newsitem.title: CHINA: China to charge two hijackers sent back by Taiwan.
newsitem.headline: China to charge two hijackers sent back by Taiwan.

text.p: China said on Wednesday it would put on trial two Chinese mainlanders who were repatriated from Taiwan after hijacking airliners to the island in the early 1990s.
Taipei said it had returned the hijackers in what it called an act of good faith reciprocating Beijing's May handover of an air pirate from Taiwan.

"We have completed the repatriation this morning," Chang Shu-ti of the Taiwan cabinet's Mainland Affairs Council said after the two hijackers, a man and a woman, were handed over earlier on Wednesday to Red Cross officials from the nearby mainland province of Fujian.
Chinese state television showed police leading away Han Fengying and Huang Shugang, who served out prison sentences for air piracy in Taiwan, after they arrived at a port in Fujian.
The two would be put on trial in the provinces of Guangdong and Shandong and were expected to face charges that carry the death penalty, state television said.
"Our judicial departments will pursue them according to criminal law," the television said.
China said it hoped authorities on the Nationalist-ruled island of Taiwan would hand back all hijackers it still holds.

"We hope the relevant Taiwan institutions, to assist in the smashing of hijacking crimes and to protect the lives and property of people on the two sides of the strait, will return all of the suspects in hijackings on the mainland," state television said.

The handover, conducted in a harbour in the Taiwan-held island of Quemoy, or Jinmen, just a few km (miles) off the Fujian coast, was completed despite the lack of a repatriation pact between Taipei and Beijing, which have been arch rivals since the end of the civil war in 1949.

Taipei urged Beijing to adhere to the principles of humanity, security and convenience when handling the case. The first hijacker repatriation across the Taiwan strait was in May, when Beijing handed over Liu Shan-chung, a jobless journalist who hijacked a jetliner to the Fujian port of Xiamen in March, alleging he faced persecution in Taiwan. Taiwan still holds 14 of the 16 mainlanders who hijacked 12 mainland planes to Taiwan in 1993-1994 before China tightened airport security.

Huang Shugang, a buyer for a Chinese steel factory, hijacked at gunpoint an airliner carrying 204 people to Taiwan in April 1993 after it took off on a flight from Shenzhen in southern Guangdong province.
Han Fengying was involved in the hijack of an airliner from Jinan in eastern Shandong province in September 1993.

Han's son, whom she brought when she and her husband hijacked the jet from the mainland, was not handed over but remained in foster care in Taiwan, where Han's husband has not yet completed his prison sentence.
Taiwan and China, which have no formal links since the 1949 split, reached consensus on hijacker repatriation in 1995 but did not sign the accord due to subsequent political friction.
Beijing froze bilateral negotiations 24 months ago to protest a landmark private visit to the United States by Taiwan President Lee Teng-hui in mid-1995.
